newsitem.title: PERU: Japanese official pushes for progress in Peru talks.
newsitem.headline: Japanese official pushes for progress in Peru talks.

text.p: A top envoy from Tokyo met with Peru's President Alberto Fujimori on Tuesday to push for progress in negotiations to free 72 hostages held by leftist guerrillas in the Japanese ambassador's residence.

Amid signs Japan was worried about hawkish voices in the Peruvian military urging a violent foray into the besieged house, Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura met for two hours with Fujimori in the presidential palace.

A Japanese diplomat said Komura reiterated the need for a peaceful solution to the siege, which began when Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed an embassy cocktail party on Dec. 17 and took all the guests hostage.

"He is here to keep the spirit of the talks going and to recall the commitment to a peaceful solution made in Toronto by our prime minister and President Fujimori," the diplomat said. Fujimori pledged to seek a peaceful end to the crisis in a meeting with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in January.

The main reason for Komura's three-nation visit to Latin America was to arrange for asylum in Cuba and the Dominican Republic for all or some of the rebels in exchange for handing over the hostages unharmed, the diplomat said.

"There are many purposes to this visit but the emphasis is on Cuba and the Dominican Republic, where Mr Komura will visit this week. First he must discuss the issue in Peru with the parties concerned," he told Reuters.

Komura was not expected to have any direct contact with the Cuban-inspired MRTA, which demands freedom for all of its roughly 450 imprisoned comrades in exchange for the hostages. He did meet with one of three members of a mediation panel, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, who described the session as "very positive."
Komura was to meet relatives of hostages at a Japanese cultural centre on Wednesday and leave for Cuba on Thursday.

Fujimori, grappling with the most serious challenge to his authority since taking office in 1990, has been pulled in opposite directions by his military and by Japan, which has two dozen VIP citizens inside the residence.

While some of his military and security advisers have pressed for force, even building a tunnel under the residence and practicing SWAT manoeuvres for that purpose, the Japanese have insisted on putting the lives of the hostages first.

The scant progress in talks has added to speculation that Fujimori, who is credited with smashing the guerrilla groups that once ravaged Peru, might be tempted to use force. He went to Cuba in February to arrange for asylum for at least some of the rebels if they surrender their captives.

With talks crawling ahead, government negotiator Domingo Palermo told reporters late on Monday he did not know when Latin America's longest hostage siege would end. "Nobody can fix a time limit for such a delicate subject," he said.

More than 500 captives were taken when about 20 jungle-trained rebels blew a hole in the residence's outer wall and swarmed into the building in a fierce shootout. But they gradually released most, keeping those considered valuable as bargaining chips including Fujimori's brother and two of his Cabinet ministers. Of the 72 who remain 24 are Japanese citizens, one is Bolivian and the rest are Peruvian.
